reader.title: Threatened lynching of F. H. Moberay
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: A Denver wire dispatch says the countrymen of a Mexican man shot by railroad employee F. H. Moberay at Caracas were 'about to lynch' him before he was taken to the Chama jail, so the episode is a threatened lynching; no one was lynched (A7, A1, A2).
Every report is the same Denver dispatch reprinted with small wording changes (A1, A2, A7, A3-A6, A8, A9); no local or independent account was found.

summary.text: The threatened lynching of F. H. Moberay took place at Caracas, Colorado, in March 1882, when a crowd of Mexicans threatened to lynch a Denver & Rio Grande Railroad employee who had shot two Mexican men, killing one, in a dispute over a debt.
Moberay was taken to the Chama jail for safety and escaped from it.
The story reached the press as a single Denver wire dispatch, reprinted across the country for a few days.
According to the dispatch, Moberay owed Mexican men at Caracas $4 and offered to pay it, but they demanded $8.
The papers did not give Moberay's race, or the names of the Mexican men.
The dispute ended with the Mexicans beating Moberay, who, in the dispatch's words, shot them "in self-defense," killing one and dangerously wounding another.
Because of "the high position of the Mexicans," the dispatch said, a "bitter feeling" arose among "their countrymen," who were "about to lynch" him.
He was then taken to the Chama jail "for safety," and he escaped from there.
No report of an inquest, a charge against Moberay, or his recapture appears in the coverage.

The story first ran on 21 March 1882 under a Denver, March 20 dateline in the New-York Tribune ("Two Mexicans Shot"), the Wheeling Register, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Daily Los Angeles Herald ("Fatal Dispute About Money").
The Lancaster Daily Intelligencer ran it the same day as "Four Dollars' Worth of Life," and the Salt Lake Herald put it in a column of telegraphed crimes beside the killing of Morgan Earp.
The Eureka Daily Sentinel printed it on 22 March, the Helena Weekly Herald on 23 March and the Corvallis Gazette, in a one-sentence form, on 24 March.
Every paper repeated the self-defense account without attributing it to anyone, and some called the Mexicans "this element."
The name varied from paper to paper: Moberay, Mobray, Maubry and Mawbry, with the initials F. H. or F. P.
The Helena Weekly Herald said that a single Mexican had only "attempted to beat" him.

accounts.label: Denver wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Moberay offered to pay the $4 he owed, the Mexicans demanded $8 and beat him, and he shot them in self-defense; their countrymen were about to lynch him, and he was jailed at Chama for safety and escaped.

framing.detail: Papers from New York to Nevada ran the Denver dispatch nearly verbatim under headlines such as 'Two Mexicans Shot', 'Four Dollars' Worth of Life' and 'A Shooting Affray in Colorado', accepting the self-defense version and calling the Mexicans 'this element'.

conflicts.note: The same dispatch in different papers; the differences are telegraph or typesetting variants, and no report settles the spelling.

versions.value: 'the Mexicans' (plural) beat him and he shot them
'the Mexican' (singular) beat him, or 'attempted to beat' him

conflicts.note: Reprint variants; all texts agree that one Mexican was killed and another wounded.
Most reprints carry March 20; the Eureka paper's March 21 dateline is probably its own receipt date.

record_check.dossier: lynching (threatened): the crowd threatened to lynch Moberay; the beating was part of the debt dispute between Moberay and two Mexicans, not a mob attack
Not taken from custody: he was threatened before he was jailed, was taken to the Chama jail for safety, and escaped
threat to lynch by a crowd; the beating was by the two Mexicans in the debt dispute, before Moberay shot them
One Mexican killed (by Moberay); none killed by the crowd
Moberay's race is not stated; the men he shot are called Mexicans; no Black person appears in any report

info: On or before 20 March 1882 (dispatch datelined Denver, March 20; the Eureka text is datelined March 21); exact date not given
Caracas, Colorado; Moberay was then held at the Chama jail

F. H. Moberay (also printed F. P. Maubry, F. P. Mawbry, F. H. Mobray), a Denver & Rio Grande Railroad employee, was the man the crowd threatened to lynch; his race is not stated. One Mexican was killed and another dangerously wounded by Moberay's shots; neither is named.
No formal charge is reported; the crowd's anger followed Moberay's shooting of two Mexicans, one fatally, which the dispatch says was in self-defense
